newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS-Hungary's Horn seen unscathed by scandal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Hungary's Horn seen unscathed by scandal.

text.p: Hungarian Prime Minister Gyula Horn's appearance before a parliamentary panel investigating a 1996 privatisation scandal was seen by analysts as a victory for democracy but a lost opportunity for the committee.

The committee, formed last December, is looking into the so-called "Tocsik affair", in which Marta Tocsik, an adviser to state privatisation agency APV, received 800 million forints ($4.6 million) for negotiating land deals with municipalities on APV's behalf.
The discovery of the payments led Horn to dismiss the entire APV board and the minister in charge of privatisation, Tamas Suchman, last October.
Horn's appearance on Monday was the first time in post-communist Hungary that a prime minister had been called to testify before an investigative parliamentary committee.

"It was symbolically important for parliamentary democracy that Horn accepted the committee's invitation to testify and that he calmly answered the questions," Istvan Stumpf, head of political sciences at Hungary's Academy of Sciences, told Reuters.
"But they didn't really push him very hard."
Horn told the panel he acted quickly as soon as he was prompted about possible illegal payments.
"(The government) ordered a rapid inquiry, the inquiry took five days and then we dismissed APV's board and referred the case to justice," Horn said.

A Budapest court started proceedings in the case in January, and at the request of chief prosecutor Kalman Gyorgyi, Parliament earlier this month lifted the immunity of Laszlo Boldvai, treasurer and MP of the Socialist Party, in connection with the affair.

Stumpf said it was unbelievable that the Horn was not pressed on his previous knowledge of procedures inside APV or on his connections with Boldvai. He believed the panel may have been intimidated by having the country's prime minister before them.

"It's a question of the credibility of the whole democratic institutions which includes the credibility of the MPs as well," he said. "If they destroy the Prime Minister's credibility they could affect their own standing."
Political analyst Attila Ledenyi said the opposition members of the committee had achieved their aims in part by getting Horn to appear at all.
"Although Horn came out of it well, the fact that television viewers saw him testifying will associate him with the affair and negatively affect his popularity," he said.
"He's not likely to get pulled further into the affair but his personal popularity and that of the Socialist Party will continue to fall."

The panel's kid glove cross-examination of Horn contrasted strongly with their questioning of the head of Horn's junior government coalition partner Free Democrat party (SZDSZ) Ivan Peto, observers said.

Peto said no leading SZDSZ politician was involved in the affair but he was grilled on a number of businessmen who may have received money from Tocsik and whose companies were registered at the Free Democrats' party headquarters. ($ = 174.9 Hungarian Forints)
